title: You Have The Perfect Teenager
author: The Daily Dad
summary: The Daily Dad reassures parents that their teenager's difficult behavior -- the sneaking out, lying, moodiness, aimlessness, challenging, whining, and ignoring -- is precisely normal teenage behavior. Drawing on Emily Wilson's translation of The Odyssey and Homer's portrayal of the moody, insecure, insolent Telemachus, the piece argues that teenagers have always behaved this way; they are doing their developmental job. The parent's job in response is equally clear: understand this is normal, practice patience, model mature emotional regulation, guide without making the teenager feel alien or broken, avoid taking it personally (because it isn't personal), and wait it out. The parent is the guide helping a child become an adult -- and the path to adulthood runs through the unavoidable territory of being a perfectly difficult teenager.
points: * All the sneaking out, lying, moodiness, aimlessness, and ignoring is perfectly normal teenage behavior -- not a sign that something is wrong with the child or the parent. * Homer's Telemachus in The Odyssey was moody, emotional, insecure, and insolent -- a reminder that teenagers have behaved this way across millennia and cultures; they are doing their developmental job. * The parent's job is not to make teenagers feel alien or broken, and not to take their behavior personally -- because it isn't personal. * The parent's job is to model mature emotional regulation, guide without controlling, and wait this out with patience. * The path to adulthood runs through being a perfectly difficult teenager -- and the parent's role is to help, not to prevent.
quotes: With all the sneaking out and the lying and the moodiness and the aimlessness and the challenging and the whining and the ignoring, it might not feel like you have a perfect teenager, but you do.
You most assuredly do. Because this is all perfectly normal teenage behavior.
He was moody and emotional, insecure and insolent. He was just like your teenager...and just like all teenagers. He was doing his job.
Your job is to understand this. And be patient with them. Your job is to model what mature emotional regulation looks like.
Your job is not to make them feel like they're an alien or that there is something wrong with them (because there isn't!).
Your job is not to take any of this personally (because it isn't).
Your job is to wait this out. Your job is to help them become an adult...which means first being a perfect (and overwhelmingly difficult) teenager.
